o: Total strength T = OR of all elements. Removing subsequence S leaves complement C with OR(C) ≤ T always; the removal is effective exactly when OR(C) < T, i.e., OR(C) misses some bit of T. So the answer is the number of subsets C whose OR differs from T. Checking examples: [1,2,3] gives 3, [7,4,6] gives 4, [8,8] gives 1 (only the empty complement fails to preserve bit 3... rather only complements with OR ≠ 8 count, which is just the empty set), [2,2,1] gives 5. With n up to 1e5 and values up to 1e6 (≤ 20 bits), count via inclusion–exclusion over the bits of T.
k: Answer = number of subsets C with OR(C) ≠ T = 2^n − #{OR(C) = T}.
By inclusion–exclusion over bits of T: #{OR(C)=T} = Σ_{S⊆bits(T)} (−1)^|S| · 2^{f(S)}, where f(S) = count of elements with no bit in S.

a.n: Inclusion–Exclusion over Bits of the Total OR
a.i: A subset C has OR(C) = T iff it uses every bit of T. Count subsets avoiding a set S of required bits: elements containing any bit of S are forbidden, leaving 2^{f(S)} subsets where f(S) = #{i : nums[i] & S = 0}. Inclusion–exclusion over the ≤ 20 bits of T corrects overcounting; subtract from 2^n.
s: Compute T = OR of all elements; list its bits (at most 20).
For each subset S of these bits, compute f(S) = number of elements with nums[i] & S == 0.
Accumulate signed sum Σ (−1)^|S| 2^{f(S)}; this equals #{OR(C) = T}.
a.t: O(2^B · n) with B ≤ 20 bits of T — about 4·10^7 worst case, fast enough; modular exponentiation is O(log n)

w: The crucial reframing is counting complements rather than removed subsequences — each pair (removed, kept) is bijective with the kept set. Verify the sign convention against [8,8] (bad = 2^2 − 2^0 = 3, answer 4 − 3 = 1). Pitfall: testing membership with x & mask != 0 versus x | mask == mask confusion; f(S) counts elements disjoint from S. Follow-up: count subsequences whose removal reduces strength by exactly the highest set bit, or handle updates to the array.
